prompt.context: A large steel manufacturing company based in Chicago called Steel Works has been facing some challenging times. They are facing pressure from competition who are stealing away customers by offering cheaper prices. Steel Works is currently exploring the option to shut down one of its three production units to consolidate operations and reduce its total operating costs.
prompt.question: Which production unit should Steel Works close down in order to reduce their total operating costs?

clarifying_info.q: What kind of company is Steel Works?
clarifying_info.a: Steel Works is a global steel manufacturing company that has several operations in the US.
Competitors include other major steel makers who offer similar products at lower prices.
Steel Works recently hired a new CEO that is open to investing in new technology as long as overall operating costs can be reduced.
Steel Works supplies products to several industries including aerospace, automotive, appliance makers, construction and roofing.

clarifying_info.q: Is the steel market growing or shrinking?
clarifying_info.a: Steel Works is operating in a growing steel market with a 5-year CAGR of 2.5%.

exhibits.title: Facility Map
exhibits.shows: A geographic map (not drawn to scale) showing three production units A, B, and C located near a Sparkling Water Canal and Lake Michigan. Shipping routes via road trucks and canal are indicated for each unit.
exhibits.data: Unit A: direct shipping route via trucks only (no canal access shown); Unit B: direct shipping route via canal to shipping location; Unit C: direct shipping route via canal and direct shipping route to shipping location; Sparkling Canal is undergoing a $50M revitalization project partially funded by Steel Works

framework: Production costs: compare cost per ton across units to identify the highest-cost facility
Shipping costs: assess logistics costs for each unit given road and canal access
Production capacity and utilization: identify spare capacity and feasibility of absorbing closed unit's volume
Process capability and product mix constraints: check which units can produce each steel type and at what maximum volumes
Investment required: estimate capex needed to bring remaining units to full utilization
Integration and execution: plan workforce, union relations, customer communication, and transition risk

questions.prompt: What should Steel Works consider when choosing which production unit to close?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers production costs, shipping costs, process capability/technology access, investment needed to ramp up remaining units, and integration execution. Exceptional answers also note whether product re-qualification/testing is needed when moving production and the morale impact of workforce reductions.

questions.prompt: Develop a new production plan and calculate the impact on total production costs if Steel Works closes one unit.
questions.guidance: Candidate should first compute current actual production and spare capacity for each unit, then determine which unit can be closed given product-mix constraints, then calculate old vs. new total production costs. The correct unit to close is C, because A and B together can absorb all volume within capacity and product constraints. Candidate should also note that the plan requires running both A and B at 100% utilization, and that closing C (a unionized facility) may create labor obstacles.

math.setup: Current utilization: A=80% of 2M tons=1.6M; B=90% of 4M tons=3.6M; C=80% of 1M tons=0.8M. Spare capacity: A=0.4M, B=0.4M, C=0.2M. Production cost: A=$300/ton, B=$100/ton, C=$250/ton.
steps: Old production cost A: 1.6M tons x $300 = $480M
Old production cost B: 3.6M tons x $100 = $360M
Old production cost C: 0.8M tons x $250 = $200M
New plan closes C; A runs at 2M tons (full capacity), B runs at 4M tons (full capacity)
math.answer: New total production cost = $1,000M; savings of $40M vs. current $1,040M

questions.prompt: Exhibit 3 shows shipping costs for each production unit. How does this affect the choice of which unit to close?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that Unit A has the highest shipping cost ($200/ton to send product to B or C for onward shipping) but that this does not change the recommendation to close C, because the production constraints still require keeping A and B open. An advanced candidate will recalculate total operating costs including shipping and confirm the net savings.

math.setup: Shipping costs from Exhibit 3: A=$200/ton (ships to B or C); B=$105/ton via canal; C=$100/ton via canal + $50/ton via truck, with equal split so C effective shipping = ($100+$50)/2 = $75/ton average — but the casebook uses stated totals per unit directly. Old operating costs (production + shipping) per unit taken from casebook guidance.
steps: Old operating cost A: production $480M + shipping (1.6M x $200) $320M = $800M
Old operating cost B: production $360M + shipping (3.6M x $105) $378M = $738M
Old operating cost C: production $200M + shipping (0.8M x $100 canal + 0.8M/2 x $50 truck, equal split so 0.4M x $100 + 0.4M x $50) = $200M + $40M + $20M = $260M... casebook states $320M total for C
New operating cost A: 2M x $300 + 2M x $200 = $600M + $400M = $1,000M
New operating cost B: 4M x $100 + 4M x $105 = $400M + $420M = $820M
math.answer: Net operating cost savings including shipping = $38M. Recommendation to close Unit C stands.

questions.prompt: What factors should Steel Works consider when integrating the remaining production units?
questions.guidance: Expected factors: whether the workforce has the right skills for new machinery/technology; layoff count and compensation structure; relocation of workforce; capital investment to run units at 100% utilization. Advanced factors: employee morale mitigation; customer communication about sourcing from a different unit; product testing/re-qualification; union issues from closing a unionized facility; disposition of truck fleet used by Unit C.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should Steel Works consider when integrating different production units after the closure?

categories.name: Workforce
ideas: Do remaining employees have skills to operate machinery at the absorbed unit?
How many workers will be laid off and what is the severance structure?
Will any workforce be relocated to Units A or B?
How will Steel Works manage unionized workforce at the closed Unit C?
How can management maintain morale across the company?

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Is there investment needed to bring Units A and B to 100% utilization?
Are facilities physically set up to handle increased headcount and throughput?
Will products moving between units require re-qualification or testing?
What happens to the truck fleet used by Unit C?

categories.name: Customers
ideas: Do customers need to be notified that their steel will come from a different unit?
Will aerospace/automotive customers require re-certification of product source?
Can Steel Works maintain delivery timelines during the transition?

categories.name: Cost & Investment
ideas: Is $38M in annual savings sufficient given transition costs?
Are there additional inefficiencies in process or labor that could be addressed?
Should Steel Works invest in equipment to increase Complex Phase Steel capacity?
Could building a shipping facility at Unit A eliminate inter-unit shipping costs?

categories.name: Strategic
ideas: Closing a unit reduces flexibility if demand spikes beyond combined A+B capacity
Rising demand for Complex Phase Steels may strain the 0.3M ton cap at A and B
Canal revitalization project ($50M partial funding) changes shipping economics long-term

recommendation: Close Production Unit C. It has the highest cost per ton among the two smaller units ($250/ton vs. $100/ton at B) and its 0.8M tons of volume can be absorbed by Units A and B running at full capacity within product-mix constraints.
Total operating cost savings (including shipping) are $38M per year, reducing total operating costs from $1.858B to $1.820B.
Shipping costs do not change the recommendation: although Unit A has the highest per-ton shipping cost, production constraints require keeping both A and B open.
risks: Loss of employee morale from closing a unionized facility; potential labor action or litigation
Units A and B will need to run at 100% utilization, leaving no buffer for demand spikes or downtime
Growing demand for Complex Phase Steels could strain the maximum 0.3M ton capacity at each of A and B
$38M in savings may be insufficient relative to transition and one-time closure costs
next_steps: Communicate facility closure plans to customers of Unit C and ensure continuity of supply
Form a planning team to manage closure timeline, workforce transition, and union negotiations
Evaluate capital investment needed at A and B to support full-capacity reliable operations
Assess whether additional investment in Complex Phase Steel capacity at A or B is warranted given market growth
Explore further cost reduction opportunities: process inefficiencies, labor productivity, and eliminating inter-unit shipping by building a dedicated shipping facility at Unit A
